Where it began

Virender Sehwag was born in Delhi on 20 October 1978 and grew up in Najafgarh, in the south-west of the city, which later gave him his nickname, the Nawab of Najafgarh. He played his first first-class cricket for Delhi in the 1997–98 season.

His start in international cricket was quiet. In his first one-day game, against Pakistan at Mohali in April 1999, he made a single run, and he waited 20 months for another chance. When it came, and especially once India asked him to open, there was nothing quiet about him at all.

The player

He made a hundred on his Test debut, 105 at Bloemfontein in 2001, batting in the middle order. Moved up to open, he became the first Indian to make a Test triple century, 309 against Pakistan at Multan in 2004. In 2008 he went further, with 319 against South Africa at Chennai, reaching 300 in just 278 balls. A year later he made 293 against Sri Lanka in Mumbai and passed 250 in only 207 balls.

Across 104 Tests he scored 8,586 runs at 49.34, with 23 hundreds, and his part-time bowling brought him 40 wickets, with a best of 5 for 104. In one-day cricket he made 219 against the West Indies at Indore in December 2011.

What made him special

He attacked from the first ball, backed away to free his arms, and cut and drove through the off side with tremendous power. Wisden called him the most exciting opener in the world in 2005, and when he got in he tended to stay: once he reached a hundred, he often turned it into 150 or more.

He did most of his damage in a match's first innings, while the pitch was fresh; his figures in the second were more modest. Yet when India needed him to dig in, he could do that too, as his patient 151 to save the Adelaide Test in the 2007–08 series showed.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him its Leading Cricketer in the World for 2008 and again for 2009, the first Indian to be chosen. He was the ICC Test Cricketer of the Year in 2010, and he received the Arjuna Award and the Padma Shri. In 2011 he opened the Sehwag International School in Jhajjar, in Haryana, and in 2017 the Delhi association named a gate at the Arun Jaitley Stadium after him.

And finally

He liked to sing to himself while he batted, and his favourite for the purpose was the Kishore Kumar song Chala Jaata Hoon. The bowlers, watching another four race away, were probably not in the mood to join in.
